articles.headline: Our Black Hills Trip.
articles.text:
Deadwood! What a flood of articles telling of hardships and affluence, misery and delirious joy, hope and despondency the sight of the city brought to our mind. Like every mining camp, the mines and miners about Deadwood have had their ups and down, but through it all, through fire and flood even, Deadwood, although twice almost swept out of existence, is still the queen city of the Hills, a bright gem sending forth its refreshing rays through the whole Hills country.

Deadwood gulch was discovered in November of 1876, by a number of miners who had come from Custer City to avoid the act of evictment which compelled all miners to leave the Hills by August 15, 1875, as the Hills was at that time a part of the Sioux reservation. The ground upon which Deadwood now stands was located under the name of Lost District and all up and down Deadwood gulch were located placer mines which have yielded enough money for a circulating medium as large as that of the United States. Fortunes of hundreds of thousands of dollars were taken out of a space scarcely larger than a grave, while the claims on either side might not furnish even enough disappointed hopes with which to line it.

In spite of the fact that the Sioux treaty was not ratified until February of 1877, Deadwood city was laid out in April, of 1876. Several curious complications have arisen in respect to the title of the lands, as mining claims everywhere take precedence and the only legal and binding title is a bed rock title deeded to a purchaser from the original locator of the mineral claim. No man without this title is safe for a moment as his whole property is liable to be located at any time and sluiced down stream piecemeal, leaving the house standing on stilts on a quartz vein for instance, which in turn is liable to be located as a quartz claim and a shaft hundreds of feet deep sunk directly under the house. This of course is a hypothetical case but one likely to happen at any time, unless a man has bought a placer title on bed rock, which is known not to contain a quartz lead.

Deadwood deserves a far longer description than we can possibly give it, and our article must in any event be inadequate. No words can do justice to the wonderful enterprise that has built up homes and fortunes in this rugged country. Deadwood is about 185 miles from Medora, the nearest railroad point in the United States. Every solitary article that could not be manufactured in the Hills, had to be shipped this distance or a greater one, on wagons. It would certainly be expected then, that the citizens of Deadwood and the Hills get along with as few of the necessities of life as possible and do not indulge at all in the luxuries. Never was a greater mistake made. The most particular dude of New York can have every want satisfied as readily in Deadwood as he can in his native haunts.

From the narrowness of the gulch, Deadwood can never become a beautiful city, but it would be a monument to the ability of any people. One can never believe that the whole city was virtually hauled in on wagons and almost instinctively listens for the shriek of the locomotive which has so long eluded the hearing of the Hills people, but which must and soon will be heard there.

Deadwood now contains about [4,000?] inhabitants, almost all of whom are prosperous and many have large fortunes. It has all the appearance of a live eastern town, although there is no town of its size in the United States that does an equal amount of business. There are a number of pretentious brick business blocks and many dwellings which would be an ornament to any city. Two daily papers, the Pioneer and Times are ably and successfully maintained. To Dolph Edwards, editor of the Pioneer, we are indebted for much of the pleasure of our stay and no one could have more thoroughly impressed us with the resources of the Hills. He is emphatically the right man in the right place.

Deadwood has as good a system of water works as can be found in the United States, a telephone system extending to every town in the Hills and not satisfied with this, almost every place of business is brilliantly illuminated with electric lights. The sewerage of the city is excellent. Two streams of pure spring water flow in the gutters of Main street, and keep the city in first-class sanitary condition. Much to our surprise, we found Deadwood to be as orderly a city as we ever visited. Not a six-shooter did we see worn openly during our entire stay. Mayor Star and city Marshal Tyler have put a stop to all such foolishness as "painting the town red." With the concluding remark that Deadwood's annual business transactions amount to considerably over $200,000,000, we will leave the subject to some one who has more space at his disposal and more ability to do the subject justice.

(To be continued.)
articles.summary: The editor describes Deadwood on his Black Hills trip: its history, land titles, enterprise, utilities and orderliness, crediting Pioneer editor Dolph Edwards.

articles.text: The astuteness of some of our exchanges verges on omniscience. The latest we have seen, however, is "the chief." Two or three papers have found out the true reason of Theodore Roosevelt's visit to the Bad Lands—that he will make a strong fight for congress in our present delegate's place. If any common sense had been used by the writers of the articles referred to, they would see that the principal reason for Mr. Roosevelt's presence here is to get away from politics altogether. Other reasons are, that he has a large amount of money invested in cattle here, and that he enjoys hunting more than the dirt of New York's political mud puddle.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy rebuts exchange papers claiming Theodore Roosevelt came to the Bad Lands to run for territorial delegate to Congress.

articles.text: We cannot help a feeling of satisfaction over the way in which our nomination of L. N. Cary for the legislature has been received. That he is by all odds the most available man, there is no doubt. That there is a rapidly growing sentiment in his favor is also manifest. Morton county is so full of cliques and factions that it is hard to crystallize the sentiment about any one candidate, but we are assured by a gentleman who is in a position to know, that Mr. Cary is by far the most popular candidate and that he is growing in strength every day. Our informant has personal prejudices in favor of another candidate, but acknowledges that he is engaged in a hopeless fight and that Mr. Cary will win on his merits. It would be hard work to throw a club in Mandan without hitting a candidate's head and the number has been increased by several tenderfeet who think that the voters here will be so dazzled by their glittering intellectuality that their candidacy can only mean success. This gentry will get most beautifully left. It is a matter of surprise that the Mandan papers have not as yet brought out their candidates but we suppose they will in time yield to the popular will, sufficiently to acknowledge the merits of our candidate.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy reports a favorable reception for its nomination of L. N. Cary for the legislature from the Morton county district.

articles.text: One day last week a commission firm at the Yards received and sold 231 cars of cattle. This unquestionably is the largest number of cattle ever sold by one firm in a single day.—[Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: Clipped: a Chicago commission firm sold 231 cars of cattle in one day.

articles.text: Fat cattle are 50@75c higher than a year ago, while common grades are nearly that much lower. Last year at this time Texans were selling at $3.50@5.00, which is fully $1.00 above present prices.—[Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: Clipped market note on cattle prices.

articles.text: A pool of all the cattlemen holding between the Cimarron and Canadian river, in Oklahoma, has been formed. It is composed of seven outfits, and will contain, when stocked up to the limits, 50,000 cattle under its control. A board of seven directors was elected, and on August 1st a full set of officers, consisting of president, treasurer, secretary and pool boss. The ranchmen turned all their stock into the pool in their own brands and then put the pool brand on in addition thereto. The pool pays all expenses by assessment pro rata with the number of cattle held by each member. To 1,000 cattle, one man and eight horses are turned in. The annual pay roll and expense bill on the pool plan will be cut down over seventy-five per cent, as under the pool plan twenty-five men and 150 horses will do the work that it now takes over seventy-five men and 500 horses to accomplish. The name is to be Cimarron and Canadian Pool. As the brand has not been decided upon yet, we are unable to give it, but it is very probable that the brand of the pool will appear in these columns soon.—[Caldwell (Kan.) Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped: Oklahoma cattlemen form the Cimarron and Canadian Pool.

articles.text: W. A. Towers, of Towers & Gudgell, Colorado and Montana ranchmen, was married last week at Decatur, Georgia, to Miss Fannie Hillyer, daughter of Judge Junius Hillyer. Mr. Towers is one of the pioneer Texas cattle drovers, and one of the most popular and well known stockmen in the range country. We extend best wishes and congratulations.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Clipped: W. A. Towers of Towers & Gudgell (a Cow Boy brand advertiser) married Fannie Hillyer at Decatur, Georgia.

articles.text: Year by year mere weight counts for less and less in determining the value of cattle in the Chicago and other great markets. Quality and degree of fatness determine value much more than weight. A farmer or shipper will make a great mistake if he attempts to fix a price on his cattle from the prices made by other lots of about the same weight. Other things being equal, animals of good size command the highest prices, but well-formed and well-fattened steers weighing 1,200 lbs. outsell rough and poorly-fattened ones 200 lbs. heavier. Remarkably large cattle are not preferred by any class of buyers over those of medium weights.—[Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: Clipped: quality and fatness, not weight, set cattle prices.

articles.text: We see by the Texas papers that Mr. Scott, of Colorado, Texas, shipped a lot of about a hundred calves to Chicago, and sold them to the butchers at $5 a hundred, netting to the shipper $7 a head. These calves were taken from old cows on the range so as to allow them to get fat for fall shipment to markets. The cows will bring ready money, but not much of it. It seems to us that these calves, if allowed to run with their mothers until winter would have been worth more to the head than the amount realized from the transaction. Some of the old cows might die, but the chances for their living and raising one to three more calves are fully equal to the chances of death during the winter. We think the policy bad. Hold all your calves and get all you can honestly, if you want to prosper in the cow business.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped: criticism of shipping calves off the range early.

articles.text: There is a mania just now to go into the business of raising stock, and there is danger that it may be over done. Not that the capacity of the pasturage will be unequal to all the cattle that may be brought into New Mexico, but the supply of water may not be sufficient during a severely dry season. The meat question is becoming an important one in the United States, as it has been for centuries in all densely populated countries. The cheap beef of the past will never be known again in America. This does not result alone from the fact that consumption increases, but more particularly because the area of production is constantly diminishing. Lands hitherto devoted to pasture are constantly being taken up for homes and devoted to the production of the necessaries of life other than meat. Hence it has become necessary to occupy and utilize every inch of ground for pasture that is not adapted to growing fruits, vegetables and cereals.—[Santa Fe, New Mexico, Review.
articles.summary: Clipped: warning that the stock-raising mania may overdo the range.

articles.text: The cowboys are a much misrepresented set of people. It is a popular impression that when one goes among them he must be prepared to shoot. But this is a false idea. I have taken part with them in the rounding up, have eaten, slept, hunted and herded cattle with them, and have never had any difficulty. If you choose to enter rum shops with them or go on drinking sprees with them it is as easy to get into a difficulty out there as it would be in New York, or anywhere else. But if a man minds his own business and at the same time shows that he is fully prepared to assert his rights—if he is neither a bully or a coward and keeps out of places in which he has no business to be, he will get along as well as in Fifth avenue. I have found them a most brave, and hospitable set of men. There is no use in trying to be overbearing with them for they won't stand the least assumption of superiority, yet there are many places in our cities where I should feel less safe than I would among the wildest cowboys of the west.—[Interview with Theodore Roosevelt in New York Tribune.
articles.summary: Reprinted extract from a New York Tribune interview in which Theodore Roosevelt defends the character of cowboys.

articles.text: There is a universal complaint among cattlemen this year about the shortage in the calf crop. This question is a matter of vital importance, and one that should have the first consideration in the minds of our cattlemen. Various reasons have been given to explain the short crop, but there is but one that will explain the reasons, and that is a scarcity of bulls. On the ranges where the number of bulls have been sufficent and in proportion to the number of cows on the range there has been very little complaint, and the calves branded have been up to the usual number. The reason for all this trouble of an insufficient number being on the range is due to cattlemen turning their cows on the range and relying on their neighbor's bulls to bring him his calf crop, thinking he can save money by so doing, and the result is that his neighbor, who has only a sufficent number for his own use, falls short as well as the other. This is nothing more or less than robbery, and the guilty man should be brought up and tried for larceny on the same grounds as if he went to his neighbor's corral and drove off a number of cattle. In Colorado the legislature has seen the evil result of this matter, and has passed a law requiring a man to have four bulls to every hundred cows he possesses. This is a just and equal protection to all men, and a subject to which the legislature of this territory should give attention and pass a like law, and then, and not until then, will this complaint of a small calf crop be at an end.—[Springer Stockmen.
articles.summary: Clipped: short calf crop blamed on scarcity of bulls; urges a four-bulls-per-hundred-cows law.

articles.summary: Hay reported very scarce; recent rains came too late for the grass.

articles.text: There is a prairie fire somewhere near us and we would caution all persons who start them that the advertisement on our first page means business and that a little carelessness is liable to land a person in the penitentiary.
articles.summary: A prairie fire burning near Medora; the paper warns fire-starters.

articles.text: Three hundred and fifty stock cars have been ordered into Dakota and Montana for this and next week's shipment of cattle to the eastern markets. This represents over $300,000, the most of which will be immediately turned into stock again.
articles.summary: 350 stock cars ordered for Dakota and Montana cattle shipments.

articles.text: We received a very pleasant call from Theodore Roosevelt, of New York, last Monday. He has established another ranch about thirty miles down the river, stocked it and put it in charge of Wm. Seawall and Wm. McDow. He intends soon taking a long hunt in the Big Horn region.
articles.summary: Theodore Roosevelt called at the Cow Boy; he has started a new ranch down river in charge of Sewall and Dow and plans a Big Horn hunt.

articles.text: The school is now running in good shape under the direction of Dan. Williams. The funds are all furnished by subscription, however, and some of the subscribers have not come to time. The list is in the hands of Wm. Vandriesche, to whom all subscriptions should be paid immediately.
articles.summary: The Medora school is running under Dan Williams, funded by subscription.

articles.text: The dance last Friday night was an occasion long to be remembered by the lovers of a good time. There is no better hall west of Fargo and each participant made the best of the opportunity. Mrs. Ertel and Miss Dallie, of Belfield were present, besides Miss Friedman, Lloyd and Mrs. Roberts from up the river.
articles.summary: A memorable dance was held in the new hall last Friday night.

articles.text: Archibald Morton, of South Heart was in town Monday. The two teams stolen from him some time since have not been recovered but hope is not by any means given up. Mr. Morton offers a reward of $150 for their return. A full description of the horses and the men who undoubtedly stole them will be furnished by Dr. Morton, of Medora.
articles.summary: Archibald Morton offers $150 for two stolen teams.

articles.text: We doubt if there is a paper in Dakota more widely known than the Cow Boy. Since our first issue we have never met a man who has not read it, and there is scarcely a copy sold that does not do double duty here before it is sent to eastern friends. A good illustration of its circulation is furnished by a letter written to George Fitzgerald from an old friend in a small Hills mining camp, who saw his advertisement in our paper. Another illustration is the fact that we figured on two hundred and fifty subscribers at the end of the year and now, before our paper is six months' old, we have a bona fide circulation of five hundred and twenty copies and not a solitary deadhead on our list. This number may seem small to our eastern readers, but we make the assertion now and will compare books at any time with any paper between Fargo and Helena to prove our assertion that we have more cash subscribers than any paper between these points.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy claims 520 paying subscribers before six months of publication.

articles.text: James Dilley, of Bismarck, is in Medora and will doubtless make up his mind to stay. He will be a welcome addition to our citizens.
articles.summary: James Dilley of Bismarck is in Medora, likely to stay.

articles.text: Peter Book has now on hand 100,000 of the best pressed brick in the territory. He can and will sell them at rates that defy competition.
articles.summary: Peter Book has 100,000 pressed brick on hand.

articles.headline: Belfield Freightlets.
articles.text:
The following extracts from a letter written in Belfield sound rather discouraging when contrasted with the letters written from there to other papers down the line. We hope the Belfield folks will take the advice of one of her fair citizens: "Stick to it and you will wear diamonds—right from Alaska."

"There has been some freight shipped from here to the Black Hills but so far, the freight-line has proven the most over-estimated thing in existence. Stud-tables have been put in at the saloons which are decidedly conspicuous by the absence of players. True, a few new faces are seen hereabouts and even a few town lots have been sold, but that said, all said. There is a something lacking and that something is entire lack of confidence, both in the town-site company and the freight line. Meantime, everyone is watching the movements of the Black Hills freight as one does the thermometer, hoping for the best but fearing for the worst at all times. This is the status of affairs at this writing and though perhaps bad medicine, is the truth."
articles.summary: A Belfield letter reports the Black Hills freight line there disappointing and confidence lacking.

Brand: E. W. Casey & Co., Frank S. Moore, Manager, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — KC / F; range O'Donnell creek
Brand: Sloping Bottom Ranch, Lloyd Roberts, Proprietor, P.O. Medora — left hip; range Little Missouri 7 mi S of N.P.R.R.
Brand: Badger Cattle Company, Howard Eaton, M'g'r, P.O. Medora — VI left hip; range Beaver creek and Little Missouri river
Brand: Dorr Clark, Spearfish, Dakota — VVV left side; range Belle Fourche
Brand: Clark & Plum, Spearfish, Dakota — E6 left side; range Grand river; additional ZD, DZ; $100 reward re VVV or E6 ranges
Brand: H. R. Tarbell & Co., Medora — horse brand left shoulder; range Davis creek and Little Missouri river
Brand: W. N. Thompson & Co., Wm. Dantz, Manager, P.O. Medora — TD left hip
Brand: Lemoyne Cattle Co. (Limited), D. K. Wade, Manager, Medora — LC left side; range Little Missouri south of R.R.; ranch Tepee bottom; also DW
Brand: Soho Cattle Co., P.O. Medora — HO with SO; range Little Missouri river and Beaver creek north of N.P.R.R.
Brand: N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., Medora — several cattle/horse brands incl. steers bought of Mason & Lovell; ranges Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: Spring Creek Ranch, L. D. & B. Rumsey, J. L. Truscott, Manager, P.O. Medora — R; range south of N.P.R.R. on Little Missouri river
Brand: Berry, Boice & Co., P.O. Keith, Montana — 777; range south of N.P.R.R., Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: E. G. Paddock, P.O. Medora — circle-dot; range six miles north of N.P.R.R. crossing of Little Missouri

Brand: Lydia S. Fuller, Frank S. Moore, Manager, P.O. Medora — LSF left shoulder; range O'Donnell creek
Brand: Custer Trail Cattle Co., Howard Eaton, Manager, P.O. Medora — HK in circle; range Little Missouri river, Deep and Davis creeks
Brand: Towers & Gudgell, P.O. Keith, Montana — OX right side; range south of N.P.R.R. on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: Wadsworth Holley & Co. Cattle Co., M. Wadsworth, Manager, P.O. Medora — 7L, Pd; range Little Missouri fifteen miles north of Medora
Brand: Neimmela Ranch, Gregor Lang, Manager, P.O. Medora — thistle; range Keogh crossing of Little Missouri to Pretty butte
